1.pericope_label: Now, thou son of man, wilt thou judge, wilt thou judge the bloody city? yea, thou shalt shew her all her abominations
debates: Whether the doubled question is addressed to the city or to the prophet
Whether the margin sense of pleading for is admissible
What the days and the years stand for
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch divide the chapter into three connected words of God, the blood-guiltiness, the melting of the dross, and the corruption of every rank
Ellicott holds that the inevitable consequence of her acts is expressed as though it had been her purpose, since she had been so fully warned that persistence looks like design
Ellicott makes the mockery a permanent principle, the necessary result in every age of high professions with inconsistent performance
Ellicott would drop the supplied words in the last clause and refers the phrase to internal confusion and social disorder
themes: A prisoner made to hold up her hand at the bar
Blood shed where the magistrates should have been vigilant
A probation completed rather than a patience exhausted
A claim to everlasting dominion set against an overthrow

6.pericope_label: Behold, the princes of Israel, every one were in thee to their power to shed blood
debates: Whether the contempt of parents is charged on the princes
Whether the last clause means taking an inheritance or being profaned
outliers: Ellicott corrects the tense and word order, so that the princes are charged with acting each according to his power to shed blood
Ellicott reads the whole catalogue as breaches of particular commands and finds the root and climax of all in the phrase about having forgotten God
Gill notes that the verb about the father is singular though the versions read it plural, and infers that few committed it
Ellicott would render the last clause that they shall be profaned by themselves, forfeiting the privileges of a holy nation
themes: Rulers foremost in the violence they should have restrained
Lies carried from door to door like wares
Bribery in money and bribery for blood
An inheritance left to a people who had lost their own

17.pericope_label: And the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, Son of man, the house of Israel is to me become dross
debates: What the several metals stand for
Why the city is made the refining pot
Whether the good suffer in the same furnace
outliers: Ellicott explains the aptness of the refining figure from the parting of the dross and the image of the refiner reflected in the molten surface, and concludes that the punishment was for purification
Henry assigns a vice to each metal, brass for impudence, tin for hypocrisy, iron for cruelty and lead for stupidity, and notes that even these are of use while dross is not
Gill holds that silver is named among the metals gathered in because those who were truly good would suffer in the same calamity and be purified by it
Gill observes that refiners in fact treat each metal apart rather than gathering them together as the verse describes
themes: Reckoned silver among themselves and dross to God
Afflictions that had not bettered them
A national centre made a crucible
A fire that proved to be material as well as figurative

23.pericope_label: Son of man, say unto her, Thou art the land that is not cleansed, nor rained upon in the day of indignation
debates: What the land not being cleansed or rained upon means
Why the false prophets were so serious an obstacle
outliers: Ellicott reads the opening from husbandry, a land neglected and uncared for, the stones not gathered and the weeds allowed to grow
Henry canvasses four senses of the same clause, unrefined metal, teaching withheld, filth not swept away, and comfort denied, and chooses between none of them
Ellicott observes that nothing could give the people a more plausible excuse for disobedience than an opposing claim to speak in the name of the Lord
Ellicott holds that the greed of the false prophets and the effects of their counsel are set out here in stronger terms than in any other passage
themes: A measure filled by all and emptied by none
Smooth words agreed on in advance
An office that was to teach the difference between holy and profane
Rulers preying on those they were set to protect

28.pericope_label: And her prophets have daubed them with untempered morter, seeing vanity, and divining lies unto them
debates: Who the people of the land are
Whether the search for a man means no godly man was left
What standing in the gap consists in
outliers: Ellicott holds that the verse does not mean there was not a single godly man, but not one of such pure and commanding character that his intercession might avert the doom
Gill limits the search to the classes just described, since there were certainly good men in the land though not among these
Ellicott takes making up the hedge as another form of standing in the gap, added for emphasis, both meaning intercession
Clarke reads the breach as made in the moral state and feeling of the people, and the man sought as one who would exhort and reprove with all long-suffering
themes: A wall of bad stuff daubed over
Oppression running down from the powerful to their tenants
A gap that wanted one man and found none
An indictment gathered into a single question
